concepts.note: A body persists in uniform motion unless acted on by a net force, which implicitly defines the inertial frames where the laws hold.
concepts.title: First law: inertia

concepts.note: The rate of change of momentum equals the applied force, so trajectories follow from integrating the equations of motion.
concepts.title: Second law F = dp/dt

concepts.note: Forces between two bodies are equal and opposite, which underlies momentum conservation and the center-of-mass theorem.
concepts.title: Third law: action-reaction

concepts.note: The laws are form-invariant under uniform relative motion, so no experiment within a closed inertial frame reveals absolute rest.
concepts.title: Galilean relativity

subtopics.note: The Principia states three laws: inertia, force proportional to change of motion, and equal and opposite action-reaction, giving F = dp/dt (commonly F = ma). Together they define inertial frames and reduce mechanics to solving differential equations.
subtopics.title: Newton's laws

concepts.note: The 1/r² force yields closed conic-section orbits, uniting terrestrial fall and celestial motion under one rule.
concepts.title: Inverse-square law

concepts.note: Equal areas and the harmonic relation T² ∝ a³ follow directly from the inverse-square force law.
concepts.title: Kepler's laws derived

concepts.note: A spherically symmetric mass attracts external points as if all its mass were at the center, and exerts no net force inside a hollow shell.
concepts.title: Shell theorem

concepts.note: The 1798 experiment measured the tiny gravitational attraction between lead spheres, giving the first value of G and the mass of the Earth.
concepts.title: Cavendish torsion balance

subtopics.note: Newton proposed that every mass attracts every other with F = G m₁m₂/r², deriving Kepler's elliptical orbits and the Moon's fall from one universal law. Cavendish's torsion-balance experiment (1798) later weighed the Earth by measuring G.
subtopics.title: Universal gravitation

concepts.note: Johann Bernoulli's 1696 challenge—the fastest descent curve—is the cycloid and launched the variational method.
concepts.title: Brachistochrone problem

concepts.note: Setting the first variation of an action integral to zero yields the stationarity condition that later becomes the equation of motion.
concepts.title: Euler-Lagrange equation

concepts.note: Shortest or extremal paths on curved surfaces are found by the same variational machinery, linking mechanics to geometry.
concepts.title: Geodesics

concepts.note: The cycloid is also the curve on which a bead falls in equal times regardless of starting point, an early variational result.
concepts.title: Tautochrone curve

subtopics.note: Euler's 1744 treatise turned extremum problems for curves into differential equations, later streamlined by Lagrange into the Euler-Lagrange equation d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0. The method seeks curves making an integral δ∫L dt stationary rather than optimizing a function.
subtopics.title: Calculus of variations

concepts.note: Torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum in the body frame, producing coupled equations for the angular velocities.
concepts.title: Euler's rotation equations

concepts.note: A symmetric tensor relating angular velocity to angular momentum, diagonalized by choosing principal axes.
concepts.title: Moment of inertia tensor

concepts.note: Inertial forces plus applied forces do no virtual work, converting constrained dynamics into statics-like balance equations.
concepts.title: D'Alembert's principle

concepts.note: Rotation about the axis of intermediate moment of inertia is unstable, now familiar as the tennis-racket or Dzhanibekov effect.
concepts.title: Intermediate axis instability

subtopics.note: Euler's equations I₁ω̇₁ + (I₃ − I₂)ω₂ω₃ = M₁ (and cyclic permutations) describe rotation of a rigid body about its principal axes. D'Alembert's principle (1743) supplied a general way to handle constraints in extended bodies.
subtopics.title: Rigid-body dynamics

concepts.note: Any set of independent parameters describing the configuration replaces Cartesian coordinates and automatically respects holonomic constraints.
concepts.title: Generalized coordinates

concepts.note: Physical paths extremize the action S = ∫L dt, from which the equations of motion follow as stationarity conditions.
concepts.title: Action principle

concepts.note: A coordinate absent from L has a conjugate momentum that is constant, an early form of symmetry-conservation reasoning.
concepts.title: Cyclic coordinates and conservation

concepts.note: Non-holonomic or non-conservative constraints are enforced by added multiplier terms in the equations of motion.
concepts.title: Lagrange multipliers

subtopics.note: Lagrange's Mécanique analytique recast all of mechanics in generalized coordinates using L = T − V and the Euler-Lagrange equations, with no explicit forces needed. Constraints are built in, and conserved quantities follow from symmetries of the Lagrangian.
subtopics.title: Lagrangian mechanics

concepts.note: Positions and momenta form a 2n-dimensional space whose points specify complete states and whose flow preserves volume (Liouville).
concepts.title: Phase space

concepts.note: The pair q̇ = ∂H/∂p, ṗ = −∂H/∂q gives symmetric first-order dynamics generated by the Hamiltonian function.
concepts.title: Hamilton's equations

concepts.note: Introduced by Poisson in 1809, {f, g} encodes time evolution via ḟ = {f, H} and identifies conserved quantities.
concepts.title: Poisson brackets

concepts.note: A canonical transformation makes H depend only on new momenta, reducing the dynamics to a single partial differential equation for the action.
concepts.title: Hamilton-Jacobi equation

subtopics.note: Hamilton's 1833 reformulation replaces second-order equations with first-order ones, q̇ = ∂H/∂p and ṗ = −∂H/∂q, for H = Σp q̇ − L. The flow becomes a geometry on phase space, leading to canonical transformations and the Hamilton-Jacobi equation.
subtopics.title: Hamiltonian mechanics
